findings.title: Niv-Mizzet, Supreme plays a package it never casts, because the Eidolons return themselves
findings.summary: Two months of iteration on the five Dissension Eidolons, which return from the graveyard to hand whenever their controller casts a multicolored spell. That inverts the usual cost of looting and rummaging: the discard is free, so every modern discard payoff becomes an engine rather than a resource trade. The write-up prices the constraint openly at roughly two dozen multicolored cards, which is why the least-played of the seven Niv-Mizzets is the all-in home rather than a tighter Grixis shell, and it names the commanders in other colours the same package slots into. Pauper, Vintage and Premodern precedent is cited as evidence the engine is real rather than cute.

notes: The author reports two months of iterating variants and names the resulting list their favourite deck to play.
The deckbuilding cost is stated as a number rather than waved at: the Eidolons need enough multicolored spells to fire, and the five-colour build is what pays it.
The package is portable — the same eight-or-so cards are offered to Varina, Raffine, Quintorius and Rydia decks, so the idea is not locked to one commander.

alternatives.name: A Grixis shell under a popular commander
alternatives.reason: Named as the seamless fit, but passed over because it runs fewer multicolored spells and the Eidolons come back less often.

alternatives.name: Squee and Master of Death alone
alternatives.reason: Easier, but already in tens of thousands of decks, which is why the article reaches past them.

findings.title: Vraska's Sculpture tokens are creatures, and two builders route around it differently
findings.summary: Reality Fracture's Jeskai Vraska turns every noncreature spell into a 1/1 Sculpture Treasure, but the tokens are artifact creatures, so they cannot tap for mana the turn they arrive. A budget EDHREC deck tech and an unrelated high-power Archidekt primer each build around that constraint and land on opposite answers: the budget list spends the tokens on costs that tap a summoning-sick creature, while the primer adds haste granters so they tap for mana straight away.

notes: Both sources name the summoning-sickness limit explicitly and build to answer it, rather than listing the commander as a set-review highlight.
The two answers are mechanically distinct: costs that tap an untapped creature ignore summoning sickness, whereas haste lets the token use its own mana ability.
Neither source reports games played, so this is reasoned rather than tested.
Highest deck count in the Reality Fracture cohort outside Tetsuko, at 1,225 decks against a catalogue trend z-score of 4.77.

findings.title: Calamity's saddle trigger repeats, making two copies and doubling an ETB
findings.summary: A budget mono-red build is organised around the second half of the attack trigger, which runs the copy process twice rather than once. Because the commander has haste it can be cast, saddled with a cheap enter-the-battlefield creature and attack on the same turn, doubling that trigger immediately for mana, cards, removal or damage. The copy only happens for a nonlegendary saddler, which pushes the creature base toward cheap repeatable enter triggers instead of marquee legends.

notes: The primer names the exact rules clause the build hangs on and explains why haste makes it work the turn the commander lands.
From a channel that specialises in overlooked commanders, which is the targeting signal docs/SOURCES.md describes.

alternatives.name: Saddling with legendary bombs
alternatives.reason: The trigger only copies a nonlegendary creature that saddled it, so a legendary saddler produces nothing at all.

alternatives.name: Building it as a go-wide token board
alternatives.reason: The copies are sacrificed at the beginning of the next end step, so value has to be banked the same turn rather than accumulated.

findings.title: The Scarlet Witch only discounts big spells, so the deck runs rituals not cantrips
findings.summary: Spells are selected to clear the mana-value-four threshold and give red mana back, so each cast is mana-neutral or better once her power reduces the cost, with refund effects bolted onto the spells that do not produce mana themselves. Her power is then pumped by equipment that scales off instants and sorceries in the graveyard, which the wheels are already filling. The finish is an X spell whose own mana value carries the discount, and the primer gives the power threshold each option needs.

notes: Per-card notes do the mana arithmetic for each inclusion rather than asserting the deck is mana-positive.
Each finisher is given the exact power threshold it needs to be lethal.

findings.title: Uldaros cuts all ramp, because a turn-two looter beats a turn-two Signet
findings.summary: The commander's exile-copy-cast trigger invites a two-card graveyard combo, and the author deliberately builds away from it, running a looter-plus-dredge engine instead that activates at instant speed in response to graveyard hate. The no-ramp decision is argued on mulligan and sequencing grounds rather than curve: ramp muddies which opening hands are keepable. Uldaros bridges to the mass-reanimation top end by casting a cheap reanimate effect that returns a spell-recurring creature, and the manabase runs multi-type lands so card-type-counting payoffs stay live.

notes: A stated and defended deckbuilding heresy — no ramp — with the sequencing reasoning behind it rather than an assertion.
Pre-release commander: the rank and deck count are still forming and should be re-read once the set is out.

findings.title: Liliana is templated like a Spellshaper, giving mono-white its discard outlet
findings.summary: The build is around the cost of the ability rather than its effect: the discard is the point and the hexproof is incidental. Because the ability needs another creature to target, the deck backfills with actual Spellshapers that share the template and so never lack a target, then treats the cleanup step as a second outlet by running catch-up land tutors to push the grip past seven while the one-land-per-turn rule keeps the excess there. Recursion runs off Emeria, the Sky Ruin, duplicated with land-copying effects rather than tutored for once.

notes: The effort is a template observation — that the ability reads like a Spellshaper — and a worked answer to mono-white's missing discard outlet.
Pre-release commander: the rank and deck count are still forming and should be re-read once the set is out.

findings.title: Bounce beats blink for Lagrella, because recasting re-fires cast triggers
findings.summary: The argument is that cheap creatures which return one of your own permanents to hand beat the standard blink package on three counts: they mostly cost two mana, they can save noncreature permanents and lands, and recasting re-fires cast triggers a flicker skips. That last point is the whole reason the shell exists, and it is what makes Shardless Agent and The One Ring work here. Lagrella was picked last, chosen to fit a game plan already built rather than to define it, so the deck survives her being answered.

notes: The archetype thesis is defended against the obvious alternative rather than asserted, with three named and rejected alternative commanders.
The author answers a reader who pushed back on the same premise in a prior column, so the reasoning has been contested.

findings.title: The Muckslinger Gang's anthem switches off in combat, so cash in size elsewhere
findings.summary: The commander pumps your other creatures only while they are not attacking or blocking, and separately pumps creature cards you own in every zone but the battlefield and the stack. A Jund build treats that as a deckbuilding instruction rather than an anthem: it grows creatures with permanent counters, then converts power into damage and cards through sacrifice, fling effects and power-threshold payoffs, leaving the team home as blockers. Because the buff reaches the graveyard, effects that read power off a card in the yard get bigger for free.

notes: Two independent builders — an off-meta channel's primer and an EDHREC columnist — reach the same non-obvious reading, that the combat exclusion is the build instruction.
The graveyard half of the anthem is the part most readings miss, and it is what makes the power-from-the-yard effects work.

alternatives.name: Treating it as a conventional Jund aggro anthem

findings.title: Zemo's boast is the reanimation spell, so Oops All Spells needs nothing in hand
findings.summary: Cutting lands entirely lets a self-targeted Balustrade Spy mill the whole deck, after which attacking with Zemo and paying his boast free-casts three creatures out of the graveyard to drain the table. Zemo also fixes the archetype's usual dead-draw problem, because his connive filters toward combo pieces and the boast casts from the graveyard rather than the hand, so it never bricks the Oops line. Cards stranded in hand are dumped with Phantasmagorian before the mill.

notes: A written step-by-step win line with a stated reason this commander is the right one for it, rather than a list of black staples.
A second Zemo primer, kept as corroboration, adds the rules point that boast only needs an attacker to have been declared, so it can be activated before blockers.

findings.title: Cost-reduce Selenia to zero mana and her bounce loop costs only life
findings.summary: Generic cost reducers take Selenia down to one white and one black pip, and the two Defilers let both pips be paid with life, so each bounce-and-recast loop costs six life and no mana. The deck treats the draining life total as the resource rather than the problem: cumulative-upkeep creatures are run deliberately as life sinks, proliferate adds age counters to the builder's own permanents to spend life faster, and life-total swap effects reset the clock. The primer is honest that this is six laps from a full life total, not an infinite combo.

notes: The builder does the cost-reduction arithmetic out loud and caps the loop honestly rather than calling it infinite.
A second Selenia primer reaches the same colours from the opposite direction and is kept as corroboration, not as a separate idea.

findings.title: Encroaching Mycosynth lets Mairsil cage planeswalkers for their loyalty abilities
findings.summary: Encroaching Mycosynth turns planeswalker cards into artifacts, which is a card type Mairsil's cage trigger can exile, so he gains loyalty abilities without ever being a planeswalker. A caged Chandra, Flameshaper is the engine: her plus ability makes a hasty token copy of Mairsil, and because the per-turn loyalty restriction applies per permanent, each new token can activate again. The primer catalogues a dozen loyalty-ability kill routes and works through the rules edges, including why making Mairsil an actual planeswalker kills him to state-based actions.

notes: Four years of maintained revision notes, with per-card reasoning recording why cards were cut after play.
The rules section resolves five specific interactions rather than asserting the line works.

alternatives.name: Mycosynth Lattice
alternatives.reason: It makes opponents' cards artifacts too, handing the same caging options to anyone who steals or copies Mairsil; Encroaching Mycosynth is ownership-scoped and reaches hand and graveyard, which is where the cage trigger looks.

alternatives.name: Clone effects that give Mairsil the planeswalker type
alternatives.reason: State-based actions bin any permanent with the planeswalker type and no loyalty counters, so making Mairsil a real planeswalker kills him instead of enabling him.

alternatives.name: The Nevinyrral's Disk cage shell
alternatives.reason: The published Mairsil line; this build deliberately goes past it into loyalty abilities rather than repeating it.
